intro.html: Some people dream big; others get things done. The best plans need both. These words describe dreamers, playful imaginations and the hard-headed test that every dream must pass: is it practical, doable and able to last?

Dreamers: idealistic, visionary (sees what the future could be), utopian (a perfect society), quixotic (noble but hopeless). Playful imagination: whimsical, fanciful, reverie (a daydream). Doers: pragmatic (practical), feasible (doable), viable (able to work or last).

words.def: guided by ideals of how things should be, rather than by what is practical
words.ex: The {idealistic} young teacher believed that every student could learn to love poetry.
words.ctx: Her plan to feed every hungry family in town by the end of summer was {idealistic}: the goal was beautiful, but she had no money, no truck and only three volunteers.
words.etym: From ideal, from Late Latin idealis, from Greek idea, “form, pattern.”

mn.cue: IDEAL-istic: aiming for the IDEAL world
mn.text: Lila wants a world where everyone shares, no one is ever lonely and every day has cake. She is {idealistic}.

scene.alt: A girl standing on a crate cheers for a perfect world where everyone shares cake.

words.def: thinking about the future with imagination and wisdom
words.ex: The {visionary} inventor sketched flying machines long before anyone could build one.
words.ctx: Most people saw only an empty lot full of weeds, but Tia was {visionary}: she pictured a garden where the whole neighborhood would grow vegetables, and five years later it was there.
words.etym: From vision, from Latin visio, “a seeing,” from videre, “to see.”

mn.text: Tia looks at the weedy empty lot and sees what could be: rows of tomatoes and kids picking beans. She is {visionary}.

scene.alt: A woman points at an empty city lot and imagines the vegetable garden it could become.

words.def: aiming for a perfect society; too ideal to be realistic
words.ex: In their {utopian} town, no door had a lock and no neighbor ever argued.
words.ctx: The club’s {utopian} plan, a school with no rules, no homework and no arguments, sounded wonderful, but no one could explain how it would actually work.
words.etym: From Utopia, a perfect imaginary island in a book of 1516; the name means “no place” in Greek (ou, not + topos, place).

mn.cue: YOU-TOPIA: a perfect place that is NO place
mn.text: On Pip’s map of the perfect island, the rivers are lemonade and nobody ever argues. Lovely, but it’s no real place: a {utopian} dream.

scene.alt: A boy on a tiny island holds up a map of a perfect land under a rainbow.

words.def: hopelessly idealistic and impractical, in a noble or romantic way
words.ex: His {quixotic} plan was to clean every beach in the state by himself.
words.ctx: Kai’s plan to buy a warm bed for every stray dog in the state with his lemonade money was {quixotic}: noble, determined and completely doomed.
words.etym: From Don Quixote, the hero of a famous Spanish novel of the early 1600s, who rode out to fight windmills that he believed were giants.

mn.cue: QUICK-SHOT: a brave shot at the impossible
mn.text: Sami builds a cardboard rocket to fly to the moon by Friday. It’s a brave, noble shot at the impossible: his plan is {quixotic}.

scene.alt: A boy in goggles salutes beside the cardboard rocket he built to fly to the moon.

words.def: playfully odd or fanciful; following sudden fancies
words.ex: The café’s {whimsical} chairs were shaped like giant teacups.
words.ctx: Nothing in the yard was ordinary: the birdbath was a boot, the gate was painted with dancing frogs and the scarecrow wore sunglasses; it was the most {whimsical} yard on the block.
words.etym: From whimsy, a playful or odd notion, related to whim.

mn.text: On a whim, Nell plants daisies in an old boot, hangs teacups in a tree and gives her cat a party hat. Her garden is {whimsical}.

scene.alt: A woman in a party hat dances in a garden where flowers grow in an old boot.

words.def: imaginative but not realistic; existing only in the imagination
words.ex: Ivy drew a {fanciful} castle with candy towers and a moat of chocolate milk.
words.ctx: The old sailor’s tales were {fanciful}; he swore he had ridden a whale and dined with a talking octopus, though everyone knew he had never left the harbor.
words.etym: From fancy (a shortened form of fantasy) + -ful.

mn.text: Ivy paints a castle with candy towers, a lollipop bridge and a dragon who serves tea. Her picture is {fanciful}.

scene.alt: A girl paints a fairy-tale castle on an easel while a tiny dragon and a lollipop float nearby.

words.def: a pleasant daydream; being lost in happy thoughts
words.ex: The ringing phone snapped Grandpa out of his {reverie}.
words.ctx: Gazing out the classroom window at the falling snow, Dev drifted into a {reverie} about sledding, so lost in it that he didn’t hear the teacher call his name twice.
words.etym: From French rêverie, “dreaming,” from rêver, “to dream.”

mn.cue: RIVER-ie: drifting off by the RIVER
mn.text: Lying by the lazy river, Lin watches the clouds float by and drifts into happy thoughts of summer. She is lost in a {reverie}.

scene.alt: A woman lies on the grass by a river, smiling, lost in a happy daydream.

words.def: dealing with things sensibly and practically
words.ex: Rather than wait years for a new bridge, the {pragmatic} villagers built a ferry.
words.ctx: While her friends argued over the perfect party theme, Maya took a {pragmatic} approach: she checked the budget, counted the chairs and ordered the pizza.
words.etym: From Greek pragmatikos, “businesslike, practical,” from pragma, “a deed, a thing done.”

mn.cue: prag-MAT-ic: put down a MAT and get across
mn.text: The path to the barn is all mud, so Dev doesn’t wish it away; he lays down an old mat and walks right over. He is {pragmatic}.

scene.alt: A teen crosses a muddy path by laying a mat over it while his mother claps.

words.ex: With three more helpers, finishing the mural by Friday became {feasible}.
words.ctx: Building a treehouse in a single afternoon was not {feasible}, so the friends split the job over five Saturdays and finished by the end of the month.
words.etym: From Old French faisable, “doable,” from faire, “to do,” from Latin facere.
words.note: Feasible means doable, not “likely.” A plan can be feasible and still never happen.

mn.cue: FEAST-ible: yes, we CAN make the feast
mn.text: Can two friends cook a feast for fifty? With three ovens, a list and a plan, yes: the feast is {feasible}.

scene.alt: Two friends with a plan and a pot cook a big feast, sure they can pull it off.

words.def: able to work, live or succeed
words.ex: Only one of the three seeds was {viable}, and it sprouted within a week.
words.ctx: The lemonade stand turned out to be a {viable} business: after paying for lemons, sugar and cups, the twins still had twenty dollars left each Saturday.
words.etym: From French viable, “able to live,” from vie, “life,” from Latin vita.

mn.cue: VI = LIFE: able to LIVE and grow
mn.text: Kai plants three seeds in three pots. Two stay bare, but one sprouts and keeps growing: that seed was {viable}.

scene.alt: A boy in a lab coat points to the one pot of three where a seed has sprouted.

after.cap: Dreams, imagination and the practical test.

after.html: Quixotic comes from Don Quixote, the hero of a famous Spanish novel, who charged at windmills thinking they were giants; a quixotic plan is admirable but hopelessly impractical. And feasible means doable, not “likely”: it is feasible to bike across the country, but that doesn’t mean you will.

opts.s: Raising the money in a single week was not {feasible}, so the class planned two bake sales spread over a month.
opts.why: The question is whether it could be done: it was not feasible.

items.q: True or false: feasible means likely to happen.
items.why: False. Feasible means possible to do, doable. Something feasible may still never happen.

choices: one boy planning to sweep every street in the city by himself, every night
a family saving for a new bike
two friends running a lemonade stand
items.why: Quixotic plans are noble but hopelessly impractical, like sweeping a whole city alone.

items.q: Which word is the opposite of idealistic?
items.why: Idealistic people are guided by how things should be; pragmatic people deal with how things are.

items.q: The word Utopia, the source of utopian, comes from Greek words meaning…
items.why: Ou (not) + topos (place): a utopia is a perfect place that exists nowhere.

items.q: Type the noun for a pleasant daydream.
items.why: A reverie is a happy daydream, from French rêver, to dream.
